_comment: DBE Grade 12 Mathematical Literacy P2, November 2025. Questions + marking-memo
answers extracted by reading the rendered scanned question paper (no text layer)
and the bilingual (Afrikaans/English) Marking Guidelines PDF (text layer present).
Only the ENGLISH memo content is transcribed. solution_method is the method the
MEMO uses to solve each question - this is the content signal the matcher links
against, not the surface wording of the question. memo_answer is verbatim from
the guidelines (decimal commas kept, South African convention).
CONTEXT CONVENTION: Mathematical Literacy questions hang off shared scenario/
resource boxes. The full scenario (tables/plans/pictures described in bracketed
words) is transcribed verbatim inside the text of the FIRST sub-question of each
block, prefixed 'CONTEXT for ...'. Later sub-questions carry a short pointer.
ANNEXURE NOTE: From 2025 the annexures are printed inside a 17-page SPECIAL
ANSWER BOOK which is NOT in the repo. This paper references ANNEXURE A (tour-bus
route map with 18 stops), ANNEXURE B (floor plans of two flats), ANNEXURE C
(map of the tracked flamingo flight) and ANNEXURE D (bookcase diagrams 1 and 2).
Annexure-dependent data below is RECONSTRUCTED from the values the memo uses;
such questions carry '[ANNEXURE ... in Special Answer Book - not in repo]' in
their text and checkable:false where the reading itself cannot be verified.
To be verified when the answer book arrives (queue row exists).

questions.text: CONTEXT for 1.1 (Q1.1.1-1.1.5): TABLE 1 below contains a list of statements and definitions of concepts used in Mathematical Literacy. [TABLE 1: STATEMENTS AND DEFINITIONS OF CONCEPTS. A: The three-dimensional space that is occupied by a gas, liquid or solid substance. B: Visual representation of the exterior sides of a building. C: Diagram of a real-life object drawn to scale. D: The region covered by the shape or object. E: The result of speed, in km/h, multiplied by the time, in hours. F: Distance around the outside of a shape. G: Scale where one unit on the map represents 50 000 units in reality. H: Shows the design and dimensions of the inside of a building, viewed from the top. I: The area of all the faces of an object added together. J: The result of speed, in km/h, divided by the time, in hours.] Use TABLE 1 above and match an explanation or a definition with EACH of the concepts below. Write only the letter (A-J) next to the question numbers (1.1.1 to 1.1.5), e.g. 1.1.6 K. QUESTION: Elevation plan
questions.memo_working: 2A correct option; answer only full marks

[Context 1.1: TABLE 1 concept definitions - see Q1.1.1] Volume
[Context 1.1: TABLE 1 concept definitions - see Q1.1.1] Distance
[Context 1.1: TABLE 1 concept definitions - see Q1.1.1] Perimeter

CONTEXT for 1.2 (Q1.2.1-1.2.4): Shown below is the information regarding a South African Airways flight from Cape Town to Johannesburg. [Flight information card: South African Airways, Wednesday 8 January 2025. Distance 1 278 km. Aircraft Boeing 737-800. Codeshare NZ 3120. Flight number: SA332. Maximum number of passengers: 189. Departure 12:15 Cape Town; Arrival 14:15 Johannesburg.] [Adapted from https://www.flysaa.com] Use the information above to answer the questions that follow. QUESTION: State, in words, the arrival time of the flight using the 12-hour format.
questions.memo_answer: Quarter past two in the afternoon. OR Fifteen minutes after two in the afternoon.
questions.memo_working: 1RT correct time in words; 1A correct time of day

questions.text: [Context 1.2: SAA flight information - see Q1.2.1] Only 33 1/3 % of the maximum number of passengers were on board this flight. Calculate the number of passengers on this flight.
questions.memo_working: Number of passengers = 33 1/3 % x 189 (1MA multiply with 33 1/3 %) = 63 (1A simplification). OR 1/3 x 189 = 63

questions.text: [Context 1.2: SAA flight information - see Q1.2.1] Write down which ONE of the methods below is the CORRECT method to calculate the speed in km/h of the aircraft. Write only the letter (A-C) next to the question number (1.2.3). A: 1 278 / 14:15. B: 1 278 / 2. C: 2 / 1 278.
questions.memo_note: Flight time = 12:15 to 14:15 = 2 hours, so speed = 1 278 km ÷ 2 h.

questions.text: [Context 1.2: SAA flight information - see Q1.2.1] State which day of the week was 26 December 2024.
questions.memo_note: Working back from Wednesday 8 January 2025: 1 January 2025 was a Wednesday, so 25 December 2024 was a Wednesday and 26 December 2024 a Thursday. Verified against the real calendar.

questions.text: CONTEXT for 1.3 (Q1.3.1-1.3.3): One way to save money during winter is to wrap the geyser and waterpipes with a geyser blanket. A geyser blanket is made of aerolite which can easily be cut. The pictures below show the steps to wrap the geyser in aerolite. [Six labelled pictures arranged P -> Q -> R (top row) and U <- T <- S (bottom row): P person cutting/measuring a roll of aerolite; Q person cutting a circular shape from aerolite; R person laying a circle flat on a sheet; S person carrying/gluing a circular piece; T person rolling aerolite around a cylinder; U person taping/fixing aerolite around pipes.] [Adapted from www.21homeinsulations.co.za] NOTE: Aerolite is insulating material that allows heat to stay in an object. Use the information above to answer the questions that follow. QUESTION: Write down the letter (P-U) of the picture that matches EACH of the following statements: (a) Cut out circles of the aerolite to be placed on both ends of the geyser. (b) Apply glue to the circular pieces of the aerolite. (c) The strips of aerolite are wrapped around the pipes. (d) Roll the aerolite around the lateral surface of the geyser. (e) Use duct tape to secure the aerolite around the lateral surface. (f) Attach the circular pieces of the aerolite to the geyser.
questions.memo_answer: (a) R; (b) S; (c) U; (d) P; (e) Q; (f) T

questions.text: [Context 1.3: geyser blanket steps - see Q1.3.1] Choose ONE of the following formulae that can be used to calculate how much aerolite is needed for the total surface area of the geyser only. Write only the letter (A-D) next to the question number (1.3.2). A: pi x radius^2 x height + 2 x pi x radius. B: pi x radius x height + length x width. C: 2 x pi x radius x height + 2 x pi x radius^2. D: 1/2 base x height.
questions.topic: Measurement (surface area formula of a cylinder)

questions.text: [Context 1.3: geyser blanket steps - see Q1.3.1] The length of the geyser is 1,2 m. Convert this measurement to mm.
questions.memo_working: Length of geyser = 1,2 m x 1 000 (1MA multiply by 1 000) = 1 200 mm (1A conversion)

questions.text: CONTEXT for 2.1 (Q2.1.1-2.1.3): The seating plan for a tourist bus that travels around Cape Town is shown below. [Seating plan: UPPER DECK, 59 SEATS - rows of forward-facing seats with row V at the rear left and row G at the front right; stairs indicated mid-deck. LOWER DECK, 22 SEATS AND DRIVER SEAT - row F and row A indicated, driver seat front right, toilet at front left of cabin, stairs at rear. KEY: Driver seat; Toilet; Forward-facing seat; Stairs.] [Adapted from www.venturebustours.com/seating] Study the information above and answer the questions that follow. QUESTION: Determine the number of forward-facing passenger seats on this bus.
questions.memo_working: Number of seats = 59 + 22 - 4 (1MA addition and subtraction of correct values) = 77 seats (1A simplification). AO
questions.memo_note: Four of the 81 passenger seats on the plan are not forward-facing.

questions.text: [Context 2.1: tourist bus seating plan - see Q2.1.1] The seats are numbered according to the following numbering system: A to F is for the lower deck; G to V is for the upper deck; the seats are numbered 1 to 4 from right to left if you are facing the back of the bus. Write down the seat number which has the easiest access to the toilet.
questions.topic: Maps and Plans (seat numbering, position on plan)

questions.text: [Context 2.1: tourist bus seating plan - see Q2.1.1] Complete the following paragraph with the directions to move from seat C2 to seat J3 by using the words provided in the list below. Write only the word next to the question numbers (2.1.3(a) to 2.1.3(d)). [Word list: aisle; second; left; right; first] Paragraph: Move forward towards the front set of stairs on your (a) ... Use this set of stairs to get to the upper deck. Once on the upper deck, turn (b) ... and you will find your seat on the (c) ... in the (d) ... row from the stairs.
questions.topic: Maps and Plans (directions on a plan)

questions.text: CONTEXT for 2.2 (Q2.2.1-2.2.4): ANNEXURE A in the ANSWER BOOK shows a route map of a round trip and the 18 stops made by a tour bus. [ANNEXURE A in Special Answer Book - not in repo. From memo usage: a Cape Town hop-on-hop-off style route map with 18 numbered stops including Camps Bay (southern-most stop), a bar scale on which 13 mm (accept 12-13 mm measured) represents 500 m, and a loop travelled clockwise from stop 11 to stop 18.] Use ANNEXURE A to answer the questions that follow. QUESTION: Write down the name of the southern-most stop on this route.
questions.topic: Maps and Plans (compass directions on a map)

questions.text: [Context 2.2: ANNEXURE A tour-bus route map - see Q2.2.1] Name the type of scale used on this map. [ANNEXURE A in Special Answer Book - not in repo]
questions.memo_answer: Bar scale / Line scale / Linear scale / Graphic scale

questions.text: [Context 2.2: ANNEXURE A tour-bus route map - see Q2.2.1] State whether the bus will be driving in a clockwise or an anticlockwise direction from stop 11 to stop 18. [ANNEXURE A in Special Answer Book - not in repo]

[Context 2.2: ANNEXURE A tour-bus route map - see Q2.2.1] The distance of a round trip is 19,2 km. Use the given scale on the map to determine the map distance. [ANNEXURE A in Special Answer Book - not in repo]
questions.topic: Maps and Plans (bar scale, map distance)
questions.memo_answer: 499,2 mm OR 49,92 cm (Accept 460,8 mm for a 12 mm bar-scale measurement)
questions.memo_working: 13 mm = 500 m (1A measured distance, 1RT correct ratio). Real distance: 19,2 km = 19 200 m (1C convert to m). Map distance = 19 200 ÷ 500 x 13 (1MCA divide and multiply) = 499,2 mm (1CA simplification). OR 1,3 cm = 500 m = 0,5 km; map distance = 19,2 x 1,3/0,5 = 49,92 cm. Accept measurements 12 mm - 13 mm
questions.memo_note: The bar-scale measurement (13 mm = 500 m) comes from the missing ANNEXURE A; the scaling arithmetic (19 200/500 x 13 = 499,2) is verified.

questions.text: CONTEXT for 2.3 (Q2.3.1-2.3.5): John lives in a flat in Cape Town. ANNEXURE B in the ANSWER BOOK shows the floor plans of two flats in John's block of flats. Flat 1 is on the ground floor and Flat 2 is on the first floor, which forms part of a block of flats. [ANNEXURE B in Special Answer Book - not in repo. From memo usage: two floor plans with imperial dimensions; the living room's longer dimension is 12'8"; the bathroom door opens to the right as you enter; Flat 1 has a living room where Flat 2 has a bedroom; Flat 2 (first floor) has a balcony while Flat 1 (ground floor) does not; neither plan has windows in the north- or south-facing walls.] Use ANNEXURE B to answer the questions that follow. QUESTION: State whether the bathroom door opens to the (left/right) as you enter the bathroom.
questions.topic: Maps and Plans (floor plans, door swing)

questions.text: [Context 2.3: ANNEXURE B floor plans of two flats - see Q2.3.1] Convert the longer dimension of the living room to centimetres. [ANNEXURE B in Special Answer Book - not in repo]
questions.memo_working: Longer dimension = 12'8" (1RT). 12' x 30,48 (1MCA multiply by 30,48) = 365,76 cm (1C convert feet to cm); 8" x 2,54 = 20,32 cm (1C convert inches to cm). Total = 365,76 + 20,32 = 386,08 cm (1CA simplification)
questions.memo_note: The 12'8" reading comes from the missing ANNEXURE B; the conversion arithmetic (12 x 30,48 + 8 x 2,54 = 386,08) is verified. Second memo alternative prints '365,6 cm' - typo for 365,76 cm.

questions.text: [Context 2.3: ANNEXURE B floor plans of two flats - see Q2.3.1] Write down TWO differences between Flat 1 and Flat 2. [ANNEXURE B in Special Answer Book - not in repo]
questions.memo_answer: One has a living room and the other has a bedroom; the balcony is on the first floor (Flat 2 has a balcony, Flat 1 does not).
questions.memo_working: 2RT identify first difference; 2RT identify second difference

questions.text: [Context 2.3: ANNEXURE B floor plans of two flats - see Q2.3.1] Give ONE possible reason why Flat 1 does not have a balcony.
questions.memo_answer: It is on the ground floor.

questions.text: [Context 2.3: ANNEXURE B floor plans of two flats - see Q2.3.1] Explain why there are no windows in the north- and south-facing walls of both plans.
questions.memo_answer: There must be more flats adjacent to it.

questions.text: CONTEXT for 3.1 (Q3.1.1-3.1.5): Mrs Xulu used different recycled materials to make a tree decoration to hang on the wall, as shown in the picture below. She cut out different coloured circles to form the tree pattern. She made a tree-shaped template using cardboard to form the backing for the coloured circles to be pasted on. The template was made up of three sections: Part A, Part B and Part C. [PICTURE OF TREE DECORATION: a triangular tree built from many small coloured circles with a star on top. MEASUREMENTS OF CARDBOARD TEMPLATE: a three-tier tree outline with a star on top; the top triangular tier is Part A with a vertical height of 240 mm; Part B is the middle tier; Part C is the bottom tier.] [Adapted from www.pinterest.com] NOTE: Dimension of the base of the triangle in Part A = 28 cm. Use the information above to answer the questions that follow. QUESTION: Mrs Xulu took 3 hours and 27 minutes without any break to cut out the circles. She finished at 13:12. Determine the time at which Mrs Xulu started cutting out the circles.
questions.memo_working: 13:12 - 3 hours and 27 min (1MA subtracting time) = 09:45 (1A simplification). AO

questions.text: [Context 3.1: tree decoration template - see Q3.1.1] In Part A, there are seven rows of circles. The first row consists of one circle at the top and thereafter, each successive row has an additional circle added to complete the rest of the rows. Calculate the total number of circles in Part A.
questions.memo_working: Number = 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 + 7 (1RT interpreting pattern, 1MA adding values) = 28 (1CA simplification). OR 7(1+7)/2 = 28. AO

questions.text: [Context 3.1: tree decoration template - see Q3.1.1] Calculate, in cm², the area of Part A. You may use the following formula: Area of triangle = 1/2 base x height
questions.topic: Measurement (area of a triangle, unit conversion)
questions.memo_working: Height in cm = 240 mm = 24 cm (1C conversion). Area = 1/2 (28 cm x 24 cm) (1RT 28, 1SF substitution in formula) = 336 cm² (1CA simplification). OR 1/2 x 280 mm x 240 mm = 33 600 mm² = 336 cm²

questions.text: [Context 3.1: tree decoration template - see Q3.1.1] The area of Part B is 30 240 mm². The area of Part C is 1,6 times the area of Part B. Calculate, in mm², the total area of the cardboard template.
questions.memo_working: Area of C = 30 240 mm² x 1,6 (1MA multiply by 1,6) = 48 384 mm² (1CA simplification). Total area = 48 384 mm² + 30 240 mm² + 33 600 mm² (1C convert Part A to mm², 1MCA adding values) = 112 224 mm² (1CA simplification). CA from 3.1.3

questions.text: [Context 3.1: tree decoration - see Q3.1.1] Mrs Xulu placed all the coloured circles in a container as she cut them out. TABLE 2 below shows the number of circles and the specific colours that Mrs Xulu cut out. [TABLE 2: NUMBER OF CIRCLES PER COLOUR. Red 9; Green 7; Gold 28; Dark denim 8; Mixed colour 22.] Determine, as a percentage, the probability of randomly choosing a green circle or a red circle from the container.
questions.memo_working: Total = 9 + 7 + 28 + 8 + 22 = 74 (1A correct number of circles). P = 16/74 x 100% (1MA correct numerator, 1MA concept percentage) = 21,62% (1CA simplification). OR P(red) + P(green) = 12,16% + 9,46% = 21,62%

questions.text: CONTEXT for 3.2 (Q3.2.1-3.2.3): Amanda Xulu, Mrs Xulu's daughter, makes circular-shaped earrings. She sells these earrings at the local flea market. The radius of the large circle in the picture below is 14 mm. Shown below is a picture of a pair of earrings and a diagram showing the circles of one earring. [PICTURE OF A PAIR OF EARRINGS: two dangling earrings, each with a small dark circle above a larger flower-patterned circle. NOTE: Synthetic - not real. DIAGRAM OF THE CIRCLES OF ONE EARRING: a SMALL CIRCLE above a LARGE CIRCLE with radius labelled 14 mm.] [Adapted from www.pinterest.com] Use the information above to answer the questions that follow. QUESTION: Determine, in mm, the radius of the small circle if it is 4/7 of the radius of the large circle.
questions.memo_working: Radius of small circle = 4/7 x 14 mm (1MA multiplication by 14) = 8 mm (1A correct length). AO

questions.text: [Context 3.2: earring circles - see Q3.2.1] Calculate, rounded to the nearest mm, the circumference of the large circle. You may use the following formula: Circumference of circle = 3,142 x 2 x radius
questions.memo_working: Circumference = 3,142 x 2 x 14 mm (1SF substitution in formula) = 87,976 mm (1CA simplification) ≈ 88 mm (1R rounding)

questions.text: [Context 3.2: earring circles - see Q3.2.1] Amanda decides to make 48 pairs of earrings using flower-patterned synthetic leather for the large circles. Both sides of the large circle are covered using synthetic leather, while the small circle is painted black. The radius of one large circle is 1,4 cm. The synthetic leather is sold in rolls with a width of 1,37 m. Amanda buys 30 cm of the synthetic leather. She states that after cutting the leather for ALL the large circles, the remaining synthetic leather will have an area of less than 3 000 cm². Verify her statement, showing ALL calculations. You may use the following formulae: Area of rectangle = length x width; Area of circle = 3,142 x radius²
questions.topic: Measurement (areas of rectangles and circles, verification)
questions.memo_answer: Area of material = 30 cm x 137 cm = 4 110 cm²; total area of all circles = 3,142 x (1,4)² x 48 x 2 x 2 = 1 182,40 cm²; area of off-cuts = 4 110 - 1 182,40 = 2 927,60 cm². Her statement is CORRECT.
questions.memo_working: Area of material = 30 cm x 137 cm (1C converting to cm, 1SF substitution in formula) = 4 110 cm² (1CA correct area). Total area of all circles = 3,142 x (1,4 cm)² x 48 x 2 x 2 (1SF substitution, 1MA multiplying by 48, 1MA multiplying by 2 x 2) = 1 182,40 cm² (1CA simplification). Area of off-cuts = 4 110 - 1 182,40 = 2 927,60 cm² (1CA area of off-cuts). Her statement is CORRECT (1O opinion). [48 pairs = 96 earrings, each large circle covered on both sides = 192 circle areas]

questions.text: CONTEXT for 4.1 (Q4.1.1-4.1.3): A flamingo (bird) was fitted with a Global Positioning System (GPS) tracking device. ANNEXURE C in the ANSWER BOOK shows the map with the tracked flight of the flamingo, starting at point A and ending at point E. [Picture: FLAMINGO. ANNEXURE C in Special Answer Book - not in repo. From memo usage: a map of central South Africa showing towns including Colesberg, De Aar (directly west of Colesberg), Kimberley, Britstown (both on the N12), Hanover (Northern Cape), Middelburg (Eastern Cape) and Queenstown; 8 different numbered national roads; provincial borders shown as broken/dotted lines; tracked flight path A to E not passing over Queenstown.] Use ANNEXURE C to answer the questions that follow. QUESTION: Name the closest town directly west of Colesberg.
questions.topic: Maps and Plans (compass directions on a map)

questions.text: [Context 4.1: ANNEXURE C flamingo tracking map - see Q4.1.1] (a) National roads are indicated with a number enclosed in a pentagon, e.g. [N1 pentagon symbol]. Write down how many different national roads are shown on this map. [ANNEXURE C in Special Answer Book - not in repo]
questions.topic: Maps and Plans (national roads on a map)

questions.text: [Context 4.1: ANNEXURE C flamingo tracking map - see Q4.1.1] (b) Name the towns found on the N12. [ANNEXURE C in Special Answer Book - not in repo]
questions.topic: Maps and Plans (roads and towns on a map)

questions.text: [Context 4.1: ANNEXURE C flamingo tracking map - see Q4.1.1] Hanover is a town in the Northern Cape, while Middelburg is a town in the Eastern Cape. Describe how the provincial borders are indicated on this map. [ANNEXURE C in Special Answer Book - not in repo]
questions.memo_answer: Provincial borders are indicated by a broken line / dotted line / dashed line.

questions.text: CONTEXT for 4.2 (Q4.2.1-4.2.6): On 13 January 2022, the flamingo was in area A on the map. On 13 June 2023, it started moving southwards from area A, the starting point of tracking the bird, and followed the following path: On 14 June, the flamingo spent the night at a small pan at area B. On 15 June at 19:00, it flew non-stop for 14 hours and 25 minutes to arrive at area E, the end point. [Adapted from https://www.news24.com/news24/community-newspaper/noordkaapbulletin] Use ANNEXURE C and the information above to answer the questions that follow. QUESTION: Write down the number of months the bird spent in area A.
[Context 4.2: flamingo flight path - see Q4.2.1] Determine the bird's date and time of arrival at area E.
questions.memo_working: Time of arrival = 19:00 + 14 hours 25 min (1MA adding the flight time) = 09:25 (1A arrival time) on 16 June (1A). OR from 19:00 to 24:00 = 5 hours; 14 hours 25 min - 5 hours = 09:25; 16 June 2023 at 09:25. AO

questions.text: [Context 4.2: flamingo flight path, ANNEXURE C - see Q4.2.1] Write down the probability that the bird flew directly over Queenstown. [ANNEXURE C in Special Answer Book - not in repo]
questions.memo_note: The tracked flight path on the missing ANNEXURE C does not pass over Queenstown.

questions.text: [Context 4.2: flamingo flight path - see Q4.2.1] The flight from area B to area E is 770 km. Calculate (in km/h) the average speed of the bird as it flew from area B to area E. You may use this formula: Distance = speed x time
questions.memo_working: 770 km = speed x 14 hours 25 min (1SF substitute into formula). Speed = 770 km / 14 hours 25 min (1S change subject of formula) = 770 km / 14,4166... hours (1C convert minutes to hours) = 53,41 km/h (1CA simplification)

questions.text: [Context 4.2: flamingo flight path - see Q4.2.1] The direct distance between area B and area E is 311,72 miles. The person tracking the bird's GPS stated that the bird flew an extra distance of 268,13 km when compared to the direct distance. 1 mile = 1,60934 km. Verify, with calculations, whether this statement is VALID.
questions.memo_working: 311,72 x 1,60934 km (1MA multiply with conversion factor) = 501,6634... km (1A simplification). Extra distance = 770 km - 501,6634... km (1MCA subtracting) = 268,336... km (1CA simplification). INVALID (1O verification). OR 501,6634... + 268,13 = 769,7934... km ≠ 770 km; INVALID

questions.text: [Context 4.2: flamingo facts - see Q4.2.1] The biggest flamingo is 59 inches tall, which is approximately 5 feet. Some interesting facts about a country where flamingos are common: Approximately 10% of this country's women are shorter than 5 feet; women make up 50% of this country's population; this country has a total population of 333 million people; 78% of this country's population are adults. Calculate, rounded to the nearest million, the number of adult women shorter than 5 feet in this country.
questions.memo_working: Number of adults = 78% x 333 million (1MA calculating 78%) = 259,74 million. Number of adult women = 50% x 259,74 million (1MA calculating 50% of previous value) = 129,87 million. Number shorter than 5 feet = 10% x 129,87 million (1MA calculating 10% of previous value) = 12,987 million (1CA simplification) ≈ 13 million (1R correctly rounded). OR 50% x 333 000 000 = 166 500 000; 78% x 166 500 000 = 129 870 000; 10% x 129 870 000 = 12 987 000 ≈ 13 000 000

questions.text: CONTEXT for 5.1 (Q5.1.1-5.1.3): Simon is a carpenter. He builds wooden bookcases using wooden pieces for shelves and the frame, and hardboard for the back. The diagrams on ANNEXURE D in the ANSWER BOOK can be described as follows: DIAGRAM 1 shows wooden pieces for the top, bottom, sides and shelves of a bookcase, with hardboard for the back of the bookcase. DIAGRAM 2 shows the hardboard (i.e. the back of the bookcase) and SIX pieces of wood, with dimensions, that will have to be cut out to assemble a single bookcase. [ANNEXURE D in Special Answer Book - not in repo. From memo usage: DIAGRAM 2 labels the pieces with letters A-G: A and B = side pieces 90 cm x 20 cm, E and D = top and bottom pieces 60 cm x 20 cm, F and G = shelves 56 cm x 20 cm, C = hardboard back 60 cm x 90 cm; the bookcase has three shelf openings of which one has a height greater than 30 cm.] Use the information above and ANNEXURE D in the ANSWER BOOK to answer the questions that follow. QUESTION: Choose the letter (A-G) in DIAGRAM 2 that matches the item in DIAGRAM 1 given below. Write down only the letter next to the question numbers (5.1.1(a) to 5.1.1(b)). (a) Shelf
[Context 5.1: ANNEXURE D bookcase diagrams - see Q5.1.1a] (b) Back of bookcase

[Context 5.1: ANNEXURE D bookcase diagrams - see Q5.1.1a] Write down the probability of randomly placing a book on a shelf with a height greater than 30 cm. [ANNEXURE D in Special Answer Book - not in repo]
questions.memo_note: One of the three shelf openings on the missing ANNEXURE D diagram has a height greater than 30 cm.

questions.text: [Context 5.1: ANNEXURE D bookcase diagrams - see Q5.1.1a] The back of the bookcase is made out of hardboard. (a) Explain why the dimensions of the hardboard is 60 cm by 90 cm.
questions.memo_answer: The length of the bookcase is 60 cm and the height of the bookcase is 90 cm. OR It covers the entire back of the bookcase.

questions.text: [Context 5.1: ANNEXURE D bookcase diagrams - see Q5.1.1a] (b) Draw a scaled diagram of the hardboard according to scale 1 : 20.
questions.memo_answer: [Drawn rectangle] Width = 60 cm ÷ 20 = 3 cm; height = 90 cm ÷ 20 = 4,5 cm; rectangle of 3 cm x 4,5 cm drawn.
questions.memo_working: Width = 60 cm ÷ 20 (1MA using scale) = 3 cm (1A simplification); height = 90 cm ÷ 20 = 4,5 cm (1CA simplification); 1CA width drawn; 1CA height drawn; 1CA shape

questions.text: CONTEXT for 5.2: The wooden pieces for two identical bookcases are cut from ONE complete rectangular piece of wood which is 2 cm thick, 42 cm wide and 430 cm long. [Diagram: rectangle labelled 430 cm long and 42 cm wide.] Determine the area of the remaining part of the wood after cutting the required material. You may use the following formula: Area of rectangle = length x breadth
questions.memo_answer: Area of complete piece = 42 x 430 = 18 060 cm²; area of pieces of one bookcase = (90 + 60 + 56) x (20 + 20) = 8 240 cm²; area of unused wood = 18 060 - 2(8 240) = 1 580 cm²
questions.memo_working: Area of complete piece = 42 cm x 430 cm (1SF substitute into formula) = 18 060 cm² (1A simplification). Area of pieces of one bookcase = (90 + 60 + 56) cm x (20 + 20) cm (1MA total length and width) = 8 240 cm² (1CA simplification). Area of unused wood = 18 060 - 2(8 240) (1MCA multiplying by 2) = 1 580 cm² (1CA simplification). questions.text: CONTEXT for 5.3: The density of the wood is 0,75 g/cm³. A volume of approximately 0,4 m³ unused wood is accumulated each month. Simon states that it will take more than three months to accumulate one ton of unused wood. Verify his statement, showing ALL calculations. You may use the following formula: Density = mass/volume
questions.memo_answer: Volume per month = 0,4 m³ = 400 000 cm³; mass per month = 0,75 x 400 000 = 300 000 g = 300 kg; number of months for 1 ton (1 000 kg) = 1 000 ÷ 300 = 3,33 months. VALID.
questions.memo_working: Volume of wood per month = 0,4 m³ x 100³ = 400 000 cm³ (1C converting m³ to cm³). Mass per month = 0,75 g/cm³ x 400 000 cm³ (1MA substitution) = 300 000 g (1CA mass in gram) = 300 kg. 1 ton = 1 000 kg (1C tonnes to kg). Number of months = 1 000 kg ÷ 300 kg = 3,33 (1CA number of months). VALID (1O verification). OR in 3 months: 0,3 ton x 3 = 0,9 ton < 1 ton, so VALID
